Valve warns of slower Steam approvals, possibly due to AI game surge
New games on Valve's Steam platform are getting delayed due to an extended approval process, which Valve does not directly attribute to any kind of development trend.
Imran Khan
,
Contributing Editor
November 4, 2026
schedule
2 Min Read
via Valve
There's no shortage of games coming to Steam on any given day, with the recent Steam NextFest
doubling historical highs for game submission numbers during the event
. But that flood of submissions has deleterious effects for Valve's approval process to get games onto the platform. Now Valve is warning developers it may take more time for it to approve their games for release.
In
a blog post published Tuesday night
, Valve confirmed the delays and outlined tips to help the pre-review process complete more quickly. It also informed developers of some upcoming changes to the process. On Steam, to get a game approved for release, testers from Valve have to verify certain things, like the game being able to pause, listed features like local co-op working, and similar tests, though the full process is not public information. Until Valve approves these things, the game cannot be published, which
Kotaku reports is causing some developers to miss their planned launch dates entirely
.
Related:

In a Q&A section on Valve's post, the first question deals directly with the timetables involved. Asking how long it takes to review a game build, Valve answers "We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within 3-5 days. However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days. Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us. The changes above are aimed at helping games pass review quickly the first time."
From the Kotaku article, developers are reporting waiting as long as 2-3 weeks without communication from Valve on the delays. Some games get rejections for seemingly spurious reasons and have to wait upwards of another month to either explain the miscommunication to Valve or resubmit it to potentially have it rejected again.
One game,
Wheel Make It
, was
reported by the developer to have failed approval
because Valve could not figure out how to activate local co-op, which was listed on the store page. The game actually just has two players share a keyboard.
Valve does not directly name the reason for this extended schedule beyond noting that it has seen "a significant increase in submissions for store page and build review" in recent months. But combined with the explosion of new titles on Steam NextFest and
data from Itch.io
indicating AI-driving games are flooding its platform, it is easy to assume that the flood of AI games making it onto Steam is at least partially to blame.
"If you look over your store page and game build with these things in mind, and consider the customer experience of interacting with your store page and game, you should be well equipped for your pre-release review process," the blog post concludes.
